Bakelite is made from phenol and formaldehyde, and the sequence involves two kinds of step ✓
— **electrophilic substitution and dehydration**, option (a).
**Step 1 — electrophilic substitution.** The phenol ring is strongly activated by its –OH
group, which directs incoming electrophiles to the **ortho and para** positions. Formaldehyde,
protonated in the acidic medium, acts as the electrophile and attaches there:
C₆H₅OH + HCHO ⟶ **o- and p-hydroxymethylphenol**
**Step 2 — dehydration (condensation).** The hydroxymethyl group loses water and the
resulting carbocation attacks another phenol ring, forming a **–CH₂– bridge** between the two
rings:
2 HOC₆H₄CH₂OH ⟶ HOC₆H₄–**CH₂**–C₆H₄OH + H₂O
Repeating both steps builds the chain, and continued heating cross-links it in three
dimensions to give the hard, infusible thermosetting solid.
Why the others fail: **(b) and (c)** name additions, but the aromatic ring undergoes
substitution, not addition; and **(d)** names elimination, which is not what the ring does.
The fact that the ring **substitutes** rather than adds is what preserves its aromaticity
throughout — and that is the reason bakelite is so stable and heat-resistant.
∴ electrophilic substitution and dehydration.

Natural rubber is **cis-1,4-polyisoprene**, and every double bond along the chain has the
**cis** configuration ✓ — option (c).
The geometry is what makes it elastic. A **cis** double bond puts a permanent **kink** in the
chain, so the chains cannot lie straight or pack closely together. They coil up instead, held
only by weak van der Waals forces. Pull the rubber and the coils straighten out; release it
and they spring back — which is exactly what elasticity is.
The contrast with the **trans** isomer proves the point. **Gutta-percha** is
**trans**-1,4-polyisoprene: the same atoms, the same monomer, but with every double bond
trans. Without the kinks the chains lie straight, pack closely and crystallise, and the
material is **hard and horny** with no elasticity at all. It was once used for golf-ball
covers and dental fillings.
So the single difference between a stretchy material and a rigid one is the geometry at the
double bond.
Options (a) and (b), alternating or random configurations, would give an irregular chain with
neither property clearly; natural rubber is in fact remarkably regular, which is why it can
be vulcanised to such consistent properties.
∴ all cis-configuration.

a **–CH₂–CH₂–** unit, which is the repeat unit of **polythene**
alternating along the chain. So the product is an **alternating ethylene-propylene
copolymer** ✓ — option (a).

**(c) polypropylene** would require every unit to be –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, with no plain –CH₂–CH₂–
**(d) polybutylene** would need a four-carbon repeat with a different branching pattern
**(b) vulcanised rubber** is quite different: vulcanisation **cross-links** the chains with

A **macromolecule** is a very large molecule, typically a **polymer** with a molar mass in
the thousands or more.
**(c) Palmitate** ✓ **not a macromolecule** — this is the answer. Palmitic acid is
CH₃(CH₂)₁₄COOH, a single **fatty acid** with just 16 carbons and a molar mass of **256**. It
is a perfectly ordinary small molecule: it has a long chain, but a chain is not a polymer.
The others are all macromolecules:
**(a) DNA** — a polymer of **nucleotides**, with molar masses running to millions
**(b) Starch** — a polymer of **glucose**, with hundreds or thousands of units
**(d) Insulin** — a **protein**, a polymer of 51 amino acids, molar mass about 5800
The distinction worth being clear about is between a **large molecule** and a **big
structure**. Palmitate molecules do assemble into micelles and membranes containing thousands
of molecules, but those are **aggregates** held by weak forces, not single covalently bonded
molecules. A macromolecule must be one molecule throughout.
The same point separates a **macromolecular colloid** (starch or protein dissolved in water,
where each particle really is one molecule) from an **associated colloid** such as soap,
where each particle is a cluster of small molecules.
∴ palmitate.
